tour.welcomePatientBody: A quick tour of what is here and the order to do it in. Takes about twenty seconds.
tour.welcomeClinicianBody: A quick tour of the console: how the caseload is ranked, where the explanations are, and what the models can and cannot do.

patient.assessmentBody: Three steps, about 10 minutes: a few questions about you, a hearing test, then questionnaires. Everything else is built from it.
patient.headphonesBody: Tones are played to each ear separately, so speakers will not work. Find the quietest room you can.
patient.therapyBody: Sounds chosen from your own results. Press play, set the level so your tinnitus is still just audible, and listen.
patient.chatBody: The Everyday Assistant Companion knows your results and answers in your own language. It is there at 3am, which is usually when this is hardest.
patient.clinicianBody: Who is looking after you, when you next see them, what they wrote last time, and a form to request an appointment.
patient.guideBody: The full guide covers every screen, every number and every measurement, in plain language.

clinician.caseloadBody: Sorted by clinical priority, not alphabetically. The score is transparent and every row shows the reasons behind its position.
clinician.safetyBody: Nine rule-based red flags run before and independently of the models. An urgent flag is worth up to 40 points; a maximal THI is worth 14.
clinician.attributionBody: Open a patient for a per-patient Shapley decomposition — which of their values drove the risk, and by how much.
clinician.cochleaTitle: The cochlea is inside the report
clinician.cochleaBody: Quick view on any case, and the patient record, both render that patient's own hair cells with their matched tinnitus frequency marked. No separate screen to navigate to.
clinician.intervalBody: Predicted values are shown with an 80% interval and the drivers behind them, on the patient's report. Held-out metrics remain published on /api/ml/model-card.
clinician.docsBody: Methods, cut-points, guideline basis and limitations for every measurement in the platform.

firstRun.lead: Let's find out what your tinnitus actually is. Three steps, about 10 minutes.
firstRun.startSub: You will need headphones and a quiet room

wellness.question: How have you been today?
wellness.sub: One tap. Nobody is scoring you.
wellness.goodReply: Good days are worth noticing. They are data too.
wellness.okReply: Steady is a perfectly good place to be.
wellness.mixedReply: Fluctuation is normal — most people's weeks look like this.
wellness.difficultReply: Difficult days are common and they do pass. A therapy block often helps.
wellness.strugglingReply: Sorry it is a hard one. You do not have to sit with it alone — the assistant is there any hour.

0.line: The goal is not silence. It is getting to the point where the sound is there and you are not listening to it.

1.line: A bad night does not undo a good month. Trajectories are measured in weeks, not evenings.

2.line: Most people who improve do not notice the day it happened. They notice they have stopped checking.

3.line: Sound therapy works by giving your brain something else to encode. Quiet rooms make tinnitus louder for exactly that reason.

4.line: Sleep is usually the highest-yield thing to fix. Everything else gets easier once it is fixed.

5.line: Stress does not cause tinnitus, but it reliably turns the volume up. That is a lever you can actually pull.

6.line: You are allowed to have a day where you do none of this. Consistency over a month beats perfection over a week.

7.line: Asking 'is it still there?' is how you keep it in the foreground. The question itself is part of the loop.

8.line: Hearing loss and tinnitus travel together. Treating the loss is often the single biggest thing that helps.

9.line: Nothing about this is imaginary. There is a measurable region of your cochlea that stopped sending signal.

since.title: Since your last assessment
since.firstTime: This is your first completed assessment, so there is nothing to compare it against yet. Your next one will show what has changed — a fall of 7 points or more on the handicap score is a real improvement rather than measurement noise.
since.noChange: Nothing has moved far enough to call it a change. That is a genuine finding, not a gap — small swings between assessments are usually measurement noise.

since.thiDown: Your tinnitus handicap score has improved by {{points}} points since your last assessment.
since.thiUp: Your tinnitus handicap score has risen by {{points}} points since your last assessment — worth raising with your clinician.

since.sleepBetter: Your sleep quality has improved compared to your last assessment.
since.sleepWorse: Your sleep has been more disturbed than at your last assessment.
since.stressBetter: Your stress level has improved since your previous assessment.
since.stressWorse: Your stress level is higher than at your previous assessment.

since.anxietyWorse: Your anxiety score has risen since your previous assessment.

assessment.label: Assessment
assessment.title: Tinnitus assessment
assessment.lead: Three steps, about {{minutes}} minutes. Everything saves as you go, so you can stop and come back whenever you like.

whatHappens.title: What happens
whatHappens.note: You will need headphones and a reasonably quiet room. There is an optional 5-minute pitch-matching test at the end — we will explain it and you can decide then.

intake.characterMulti: Select every sound you hear — the first one you pick is treated as the main one.
intake.title: Tell us about your tinnitus
intake.unilateralNote: A strictly one-sided percept is checked against your hearing thresholds. If the two ears differ by 15 dB or more, imaging is recommended to rule out a cause on that side — this is routine, and finding it early is the point.
intake.duration: How long have you had it? — {{value}}
intake.durationHint: Tinnitus in the first year has the best chance of settling on its own.
intake.pulsatile: It pulses in time with my heartbeat
intake.pulsatileHelp: This changes the pathway — it needs a vascular assessment.
intake.somatic: It changes if I clench my jaw or turn my neck
intake.somaticHelp: Points to a somatic component, which physiotherapy or dental work can treat.
intake.hyperacusisHelp: Caps your therapy level and switches to a gentler protocol.
intake.noiseYearsHint: Machinery, music, power tools, firearms, aviation. Leave at zero if none.
intake.medicationHint: Comma separated, with doses if you know them.
intake.medicationPlaceholder: e.g. Amitriptyline 10 mg at night, Vitamin D
intake.consent: Allow my anonymised data to be used for research
intake.consentHelp: Optional, and it changes nothing about your care. Only de-identified values ever leave the platform.

hearing.savedBody: We saved your headphone setup from last time{{model}}. If you are using the same headphones at the same volume, you can skip straight to the test.

optional.title: One optional extra — 5 minutes
optional.lead: We can measure the actual pitch and loudness of your tinnitus by playing tones and asking you to compare them.
optional.gives1: A therapy sound with a notch cut at <0>your</0> frequency
optional.gives2: A test of whether masking is likely to help you
optional.gives3: The number your clinician tracks the percept by
optional.skip1: You still get a full assessment and a therapy plan
optional.skip2: Your plan uses broadband sound instead of a notch
optional.skip3: You can do this any time later
optional.note: This is genuinely optional. Clinical guidelines do not require pitch and loudness matching for an initial tinnitus assessment — it is offered because it is the only thing that makes a targeted notch possible, not because your assessment is incomplete without it.
optional.why1: The AAO-HNSF clinical practice guideline for tinnitus states that routine psychoacoustic testing is not required for initial assessment. Most services perform it selectively, when it will change management.
optional.why2: Your assessment already contains everything guidelines require: history, hearing thresholds, and a validated handicap measure.

review.detailedSub: Your full clinical summary for this assessment: overall hearing, what it means, a 3D model of your own cochlea, the key findings, observations, risk indicators and what happens next.
review.fullReportNote: The complete technical report — audiogram and calibration, every instrument score, the model's per-driver attributions and coding — is on your Results screen.
review.clinicianAlerted: Your clinician has been alerted automatically.
review.escalationsTitle: Extra questions you were asked, and why

questionnaires.offerLead_one: You have finished everything that is required. Based on your answers, {{count}} further questionnaire is indicated. You can answer it now, or skip and your clinician will see it flagged as outstanding.
questionnaires.offerLead_other: You have finished everything that is required. Based on your answers, {{count}} further questionnaires are indicated. You can answer them now, or skip and your clinician will see them flagged as outstanding.

questionnaires.skipped: Skipped for now: <0>{{list}}</0>. These stay on your record as recommended, and you can add them at any time.
questionnaires.escalatedTitle: Added because your screening answer indicated it
questionnaires.belowCut: Below the cut-point — no further questions needed
questionnaires.vasSeparate: Each scale is reported separately rather than summed.
questionnaires.psqiComponents: The PSQI is scored as seven components rather than an item total.
questionnaires.whyFewBody: Everyone answers an 18-item core. Longer anxiety, stress and sleep questionnaires are only offered if your short answers indicate them — which is exactly how these instruments are designed to be used — and when they are, they only ask what has not already been asked. You are not getting a lighter assessment; you are getting a shorter one that still covers every domain that changes your treatment.
questionnaires.thiExplainBody: <0>Handicap</0> — how much tinnitus interferes with your life — not loudness. Five items, one each for sleep, concentration, anxiety, daily activities and mood, drawn from the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory and scored onto its 0–100 scale so your score stays comparable with any you had before.

intro.vas: Four quick sliders about how your tinnitus is right now.
intro.thi: Five questions about how tinnitus affects your sleep, concentration, mood, anxiety and daily life. This is the score your clinician tracks over time — it is the one that responds to treatment.
intro.gad2: Two questions about how you have felt over the last two weeks.
intro.phq2: Two more, over the same two weeks.
intro.pss4: Four questions about the last month.
intro.gad7: Five more questions to grade this properly. Your first two answers already count towards the score.
intro.pss10: Six more questions to grade this properly. Your earlier four answers already count towards the score.
intro.psqi: A fuller look at your sleep over the last month.

escalation.anxietyWhy: Your two anxiety answers were above the level where the full questionnaire is recommended. It grades how severe this is, which decides whether psychological support is offered alongside sound therapy.
escalation.stressWhy: Your stress answers were above the recommended threshold. Stress is one of the strongest amplifiers of tinnitus annoyance, and grading it properly changes how much of your programme is relaxation work.
escalation.sleepWhy: Tinnitus is disrupting your sleep at least once or twice a week. Sleep is usually the highest-yield thing to fix in tinnitus care, and this is the questionnaire that identifies which part of it to target.

therapy.label: Sound therapy
therapy.title: Your programme
therapy.subtitle: Revision {{revision}} · {{strategy}} · target {{minutes}} · review in {{days}}
therapy.noActivePlanTitle: No active plan on your record
therapy.noActivePlanBody: Your assessment is complete, so a programme can be built from it now — the notch frequency comes from your pitch match and the level from your masking and discomfort thresholds.
therapy.noPlanBody: Your plan is generated from your assessment measurements — the notch frequency comes from your pitch match, the level from your masking and discomfort thresholds.
therapy.partialLoad: Your programme loaded, but some supporting data did not: {{what}}. Playback and logging still work.
therapy.audioFailed: Could not start audio on this device.
therapy.loggedRelief: Session logged — {{points}} points of relief recorded.

pre.prompt: Before you start — how loud is your tinnitus right now?
pre.note: We ask again afterwards. The difference is what lets the system learn which sounds actually work for you rather than guessing.
pre.uncalibrated: Your headphones have not been levelled on this device, so this block starts at a deliberately quiet fixed level rather than your prescribed {{level}} dB SL. Use the level fader to find the point where your tinnitus and the sound just blend.

player.maskingWarning: <0>You should still be able to hear your tinnitus.</0> If it disappears completely, the level is too high — complete masking prevents habituation, which is the thing we are actually trying to achieve.

post.louderWarning: Your tinnitus is louder after this session. That is worth reporting — it may mean the level or the modality is wrong for you. Your clinician will see this in your session log.

stats.levelHeadphones: level your headphones to deliver this

worked.title: What has worked for you
worked.note: Mean relief is the average drop in your loudness rating from before to after a session. "Adapt to my response" reallocates time toward what actually moves your numbers.

spectrum.title: Spectrum verification
spectrum.noNotch: Your plan does not include a notched block, so there is no notch to verify. That happens when the percept is broadband or the pitch match was not reliable enough to place one.
spectrum.intro: This is the actual delivered spectrum, computed server-side with the same biquad coefficients your browser instantiates. The dip is deliberate: withdrawing energy at your tinnitus frequency is the mechanism of notched therapy.
spectrum.chainNote: Three cascaded peaking sections reach 40 dB of attenuation. The per-stage Q is solved numerically so the <0>composite</0> width matches the prescription — cascading sections at the target width produces a notch roughly three times too wide.

calibration.intro: You need headphones — not speakers. Find the quietest room available and turn off fans, air conditioning and anything with a hum. This takes about two minutes and everything after it depends on getting it right.
calibration.honesty: <0>What this can and cannot do:</0> a browser cannot know the actual sound pressure at your eardrum, so these are <1>screening estimates</1>, not calibrated clinical audiometry. They are reliable for tracking your own change over time on the same hardware. They are not a substitute for a test in a sound booth.
calibration.transducerNote: This selects the reference threshold table (ISO 389) used to convert output level into estimated dB HL. Getting it wrong shifts every threshold by up to 10 dB.

transducer.circumauralHelp: Cups fully enclose the ear (e.g. studio or gaming headphones).
transducer.supra_auralHelp: Pads rest on the ear rather than around it.
transducer.insertHelp: Tips sit inside the ear canal.
transducer.unknownHelp: Nominal corrections will be used and results flagged as approximate.

calibration.levelLead: Start the sound, then use your <0>device volume</0> to bring it to the loudness of <1>someone talking to you across a table</1> — clearly audible, not loud. There is no slider here: your device volume is the only control that matters, and this sound is what you set it against.
calibration.levelledConfirm: The sound is now at conversational loudness — comfortable, clearly audible.
calibration.doNotChange: Do not change your device volume again after this point. Everything measured afterwards is referenced to this setting, so changing it invalidates the whole test.
calibration.channelLead: Swapped channels would put every left-ear threshold on the right ear. Play each side and confirm you heard it where you expect.
calibration.heardLeft: I heard that in my <0>left</0> ear
calibration.heardRight: I heard that in my <0>right</0> ear
calibration.ambientLead: A three-second microphone sample estimates the background level. Above roughly 40 dB(A), quiet tones are masked by the room and low-frequency thresholds come out worse than they really are — which the report will flag rather than hide.
calibration.skipAmbient: Skipping this is fine — microphone access is not required, and the report will note that the environment was not verified.
calibration.finishBlocked: Complete the steps above to continue
calibration.workingLevelNote: estimated, for the headphones you chose
calibration.personalisedLater: This is a working level, good enough to measure against. At the end of the hearing measurement we set your real reference level — using your own tinnitus pitch and the measurements you are about to give, rather than a standard tone.

audiometry.skipModuleHint: Leave the hearing test without taking it. No thresholds are recorded, so your audiogram, hearing grade and 3D cochlea will be unavailable.
audiometry.skippedSummary: {{count}} skipped or not converged — these are left blank on your audiogram rather than guessed.
audiometry.noThresholdsBody: Every tone was skipped, so there is no hearing data to save. Your audiogram, your report and the 3D model of your cochlea are all built from these thresholds, so the test needs to be run again before it can be saved.
audiometry.previousHint: Go back one frequency and measure it again
audiometry.interOctaveTitle: Added because adjacent octaves differed by {{gap}} dB or more
audiometry.instruction: Press the button <0>every time you hear a tone</0>, however faint — even if you are not completely sure. The tones will come at unpredictable intervals and some will be very quiet.
audiometry.catchNote: Silent catch trials are inserted periodically. A response to silence means guessing, and the report will say so.
audiometry.interOctaveNote: We test octave frequencies as standard and only add 3 or 6 kHz if your thresholds jump by {{gap}} dB or more between neighbours — the point where a dip could otherwise be missed.

notes.falsePositives_one: {{count}} false-positive response on {{trials}} silent catch trials — the patient responded when no tone was presented.
notes.falsePositives_other: {{count}} false-positive responses on {{trials}} silent catch trials — the patient responded when no tone was presented.
notes.retestDiffered: 1 kHz retest differed by {{db}} dB (limit 10 dB) — thresholds are not reproducible.
notes.clean: Catch trials clean and 1 kHz retest within 10 dB — thresholds are reproducible.
notes.interOctaveAdded_one: {{count}} inter-octave frequency added because adjacent octaves differed by {{gap}} dB or more (BSA recommended procedure).
notes.interOctaveAdded_other: {{count}} inter-octave frequencies added because adjacent octaves differed by {{gap}} dB or more (BSA recommended procedure).
notes.interOctaveNone: No inter-octave testing indicated — adjacent octaves were within {{gap}} dB throughout.

audiometry.manualLead: You set the frequency and the level yourself, present the tone, and record the threshold when the patient responds. Thresholds recorded here appear on the same audiogram and in the same report as the guided test.

bandwidth.tonalHelp: A clear single pitch, like a whistle or a test tone.
bandwidth.narrowbandHelp: A pitch, but slightly fuzzy — like a hiss with a note in it.
bandwidth.broadbandHelp: A rushing, roaring or static-like sound with no identifiable note.

loudness.unknown: Threshold at the matched frequency is unknown, so sensation level cannot be computed.
loudness.veryQuiet: A very quiet percept in absolute terms. Distress is being driven by attention and emotional response rather than by loudness — that is the usual pattern and it is good news for treatment.
loudness.typical: Typical sensation level for chronic tinnitus.
loudness.louder: Louder than most. Masking-based approaches are likely to need a higher level.
loudness.unusuallyHigh: Unusually high sensation level. Re-check the loudness match and calibration before relying on it.

mml.veryEasy: Very easily masked — a low-level masker will cover the percept. Strong indicator for sound therapy.
mml.difficult: Difficult to mask — habituation-based therapy should lead rather than masking.
mml.refractory: Refractory to masking. Do not escalate masker level; prioritise habituation and CBT.

note.complete: The percept was abolished entirely after masking. This is the strongest single predictor that sound therapy will help.
note.partial: Substantial reduction after masking — masking-based therapy is indicated.
note.minimal: Slight reduction only. Expect modest benefit; combine with habituation.
note.rebound: The percept was LOUDER after the masker. Masking is contraindicated — low-level enrichment and habituation instead.
note.absent: No residual inhibition. Prioritise habituation, notched therapy and CBT over masking.

match.characterTitle: Does your tinnitus have a clear pitch?
match.youSaid: You told us it sounds like <0>{{character}}</0>. One more question before we start playing tones.
match.broadbandNote: A percept with no identifiable pitch cannot be matched to a frequency, and a notch has nothing to be placed on. You can skip pitch matching — the therapy engine will prescribe broadband enrichment instead, which is the correct approach for this presentation.
match.bracketLead: You will hear two tones. Play each as many times as you like, then choose the one that is <0>closer to your tinnitus</0>. Neither will match exactly — just pick the nearer one. The search narrows automatically.
match.reliabilityBody: Here is the very first pair again. Choose the one closer to your tinnitus — there is no right answer, we are only checking that the same question gets the same answer. If it does not, a therapy notch will not be placed on this match.
match.retestPassedBody: The repeated comparison produced the same answer — the match is reproducible.
match.retestFailedBody: The repeated comparison produced a different answer. The match is recorded but flagged as not reproducible, and the therapy engine will withhold the notch.
match.octaveBody: This step exists because octave confusion is extremely common — patients often match a tone one octave above or below their real percept. Compare all three and choose the true match.
match.octaveCorrected: <0>Octave confusion detected and corrected.</0> The bracketing search converged one octave away from the tone you confirmed. This is recorded so the clinician knows the initial match was unstable.
match.howThisWorksBody: Naming a frequency is almost impossible. Judging which of two tones is <0>closer</0> is reliable, so the search only ever asks that and halves the bracket each round.
match.needsPitch: Loudness matching needs a matched frequency. Since pitch matching was skipped, this measurement is skipped too.
match.loudnessLead: A tone at your matched pitch of <0>{{freq}}</0> will play. Adjust the level until it is <1>exactly as loud as your tinnitus</1> — not louder, not quieter.
match.loudnessInsight: Most people are surprised here: tinnitus is usually only a few decibels above threshold even when it feels overwhelming. That gap between measured loudness and experienced intrusiveness is the single most important thing this assessment demonstrates — and it is why treatment targets the distress rather than the volume.
match.ldlLead: This sets a safety ceiling for your therapy. Raise the level until the sound becomes <0>uncomfortably loud</0> — not painful. Stop as soon as you would want to turn it down. Your therapy will be capped 20 dB below whatever you record here.
match.ldlReduced: A discomfort level below 80 dB HL indicates reduced sound tolerance. The therapy engine will switch to a graded desensitisation protocol and cap output accordingly.
match.ldlOptional: Optional but recommended — it sets the hard output cap on your therapy.
match.mmlLead: Now a band of noise around your tinnitus frequency. Start low and raise it until your tinnitus is <0>just covered</0> — the moment you can no longer hear it. Then stop.
match.riLead: A masker will play for <0>45 seconds</0>. When it stops, many people find their tinnitus is briefly quieter — or gone. We will ask you to rate it several times as it comes back.
match.riWhy: This is the most informative single measurement in the whole battery. A strong response predicts that masking-based therapy will help you; no response means habituation and CBT should lead instead. It changes the prescription.
match.listenNormally: Listen normally. Do not remove your headphones.
match.rateNow: Masker off — rate your tinnitus now
match.compareLoudness: How loud is it compared with before the masker?
match.curveAppears: The curve appears as you record ratings.
match.riReportedQuestion: Since the masker stopped, has your tinnitus reduced?
match.riReportedNote: Your own answer is recorded alongside the loudness ratings you just gave. They are kept separately because they can differ, and that difference is itself useful.

audiometryReview.title: Hearing test review
audiometryReview.caveat: These thresholds should be confirmed by a clinician before treatment decisions are based on them.

results.emptyBody: Finish an assessment and your full report, projections and explanations appear here.
results.title: Assessment report

plain.label: Your results in plain language
plain.whoGradeDefault: Graded on the average of your better ear against the WHO 2021 scale.
plain.noThresholds: No hearing thresholds were recorded for this assessment.
plain.notGradedBody: The tinnitus handicap questionnaire was not completed, so severity could not be graded.
plain.cochleaBody: Each dot is a group of hair cells, placed at the pitch it responds to. Red is where your hearing test found the most loss — and the marker is your tinnitus, sitting inside it. That correspondence is the mechanism, not a coincidence.
plain.cochleaEmpty: Once you complete a hearing test, your own thresholds are mapped onto this cochlea and your tinnitus frequency is marked.
plain.dragToRotate: Drag to rotate · scroll to zoom
plain.noObservations: The optional tinnitus matching step was not completed, so there is nothing to report here yet.

1.body: Your tinnitus is only noticeable in quiet surroundings and is easily covered by other sounds. It is not interfering with your sleep or your day.

2.body: Everyday sound covers your tinnitus and you forget about it while you are occupied. It may occasionally disturb your sleep.

3.body: You notice your tinnitus even with background noise around you, though you can still get on with your day. This is the level at which sound therapy usually helps most.

4.body: You hear your tinnitus almost all the time, other sounds rarely cover it, and it is disturbing your sleep and interrupting your day.

5.body: Your tinnitus is present constantly, your sleep is badly disrupted and most activities are difficult. This needs a combined audiology and psychological approach, not sound alone.

observation.pitchMatched: Your tinnitus was matched to a tone at about {{freq}} — {{band}}. Your sound therapy removes a band of sound at exactly that frequency, which is why it has a deliberate gap in it.
observation.loudness: Measured against your own hearing threshold, your tinnitus is only {{db}} dB loud. Most people are surprised by how small that number is — how much it intrudes depends far more on attention and stress than on volume, which is why treatment targets distress rather than loudness.
observation.riRebound: Your tinnitus was louder after a masking sound rather than quieter. This matters: masking would make you worse, so your programme deliberately uses quiet sound below your tinnitus instead of covering it.
observation.riPositive: Your tinnitus went quiet for a while after a masking sound ({{category}} response). That is a good sign — it predicts you are likely to get relief from sound-based treatment.
observation.notch: Your hearing has a dip at {{freq}} in the pattern typically caused by noise exposure. Protecting your hearing from loud sound from now on is the single most useful thing you can do.
observation.asymmetry: Your two ears differ by {{db}} dB. A difference this size is always checked further, and your clinician will have seen it flagged.
observation.maskability: How easily sound covers your tinnitus: {{category}}. This is what decides how loud your therapy needs to be.

risk.worsening: Chance of your tinnitus getting worse over the next six months: {{pct}}{{qualifier}} This is an estimate from a model, not a prediction about you personally.
risk.worseningHigh: — high enough that your clinician will want to review you sooner.
risk.therapyResponse: Estimated likelihood that sound therapy helps you: {{pct}}.
risk.catastrophic: You answered 'yes' to feeling unable to escape or cope with your tinnitus. That answer is taken seriously on its own, regardless of your total score, and psychological support is part of your plan.
risk.allClear: Nothing on your assessment needs urgent medical attention.

meaning.headlineBoth: Your tinnitus is currently causing {{severity}} interference with everyday life, and your hearing is graded {{grade}}.
meaning.headlineSeverityOnly: Your tinnitus is currently causing {{severity}} interference with everyday life.
meaning.headlineGradeOnly: Your hearing is graded {{grade}}. The tinnitus questionnaire was not completed, so severity has not been graded yet.
meaning.headlineIncomplete: This assessment is not complete enough to summarise yet.
meaning.hearingLoss: Hearing loss and tinnitus almost always travel together. The quieter parts of the sound world stop reaching your brain, and it compensates by generating activity of its own — which is what you hear. That is why treating the hearing loss is often the single most effective thing for the tinnitus, and why sound therapy works by giving your brain something real to listen to instead.
meaning.hearingNormal: Your hearing is in the normal range, which is common and does not make the tinnitus any less real. It usually means the loss is in a region a standard hearing test does not reach, or in the way sound is processed rather than detected.
meaning.severityHigh: A score in this range means tinnitus is taking up a large part of your day, and that is treatable even when the sound itself does not go away. The aim of treatment is not silence — it is getting to the point where the sound is there and you are not listening to it.
meaning.severityModerate: Most people at this level improve over weeks to months rather than days, and the improvement usually shows up as noticing it less rather than it becoming quieter.
meaning.pitchBuiltAround: Your tinnitus was matched to a tone near {{freq}}. That is the frequency your therapy is built around, and it is why your sound has a deliberate gap in it at that pitch.
meaning.noSafetyFlags: None of the safety checks were triggered. Nothing in this assessment points to a cause that needs urgent medical investigation.

finding.severity: Your tinnitus is causing <0>{{severity}}</0> interference with daily life{{score}}. A fall of 7 points or more at your next assessment is a real improvement rather than measurement noise.
finding.hearingAverage: , averaging {{value}} dB HL in your better ear
finding.hearingNote: Hearing loss and tinnitus travel together — treating the loss usually helps the tinnitus.
finding.pitch: Your tinnitus was matched at <0>{{freq}}</0>, which is inside the region where your hearing is weakest. That correspondence is the mechanism, measured on your own data.
finding.plan: A <0>{{strategy}}</0> sound programme was generated from these measurements, {{minutes}} minutes a day.
finding.safetyClear: None of the nine safety checks were triggered — nothing here suggests a cause that needs urgent medical investigation.

steps.startProgramme: <0>Start your sound programme</0> — {{minutes}} minutes a day, made from these measurements. <1>Open your programme</1>.
steps.rate: <0>Rate your tinnitus before and after each therapy block.</0> Two taps. It is what lets the programme work out which sounds actually help <1>you</1> rather than on average. <2>Open your programme</2>.
steps.review: <0>Review in {{days}} days.</0> Your clinician will look at your session history and adherence, and the programme is adjusted from what actually helped you. <1>See your appointments</1>.

guide.label: Documentation
guide.title: The guide
guide.lead: Every screen, every measurement and every number — what it is, how it is produced, and what it cannot tell you.
guide.patientViewNote: Switch to the clinician view for methods, cut-points and the guidelines each measurement follows.
guide.clinicianViewNote: Clinical detail is shown under 'Method and cut-points' in each card.
guide.inShortBody: EchoSense is a clinical decision-support prototype. Browser hearing thresholds are screening estimates. Predictions come from models trained on a simulated cohort. Terminology codes are proposals requiring confirmation. Nothing here replaces assessment by a qualified audiologist — and wherever a number appears in this app, that limit appears with it.
guide.needAHandBody: The <0>?</0> in the header replays the short tour of each screen at any time.

start.title: Where to start
start.intro: Everything in the platform is derived from one assessment. Until that is done, most screens have nothing to show.

assessment.title: The assessment
assessment.intro: Three required steps, roughly 10 minutes, plus optional extras you are asked about rather than given. Each step saves as you finish it, so you can stop and come back.

therapy.title: Sound therapy
therapy.intro: Your plan is a set of sound blocks with a daily minutes target. Every sound is generated live in your browser — there are no audio files.

consultation.title: Doctor consultation
consultation.intro: Everything about the human side of your care in one place: who is looking after you, when you next see them, what they wrote last time, and how to ask for an appointment.

support.title: Everyday Assistant Companion
support.intro: An assistant that knows your results, available at any hour, in your own language.

numbers.title: Your results and what they mean
numbers.intro: The report opens on a plain-language summary. Everything technical is one click below it, and nothing was removed.

caseload.title: Caseload and triage
caseload.intro: Your patients, ranked by clinical priority, with the ranking inspectable — plus your schedule and the patients who need attention today.

redflags.title: Red-flag screening
redflags.intro: Nine rules, run before and independently of the models, so a referral never depends on an ML artifact loading.

rehab.label: Rehabilitation
rehab.title: Your recovery programme

activity.sound_therapyWhat: Listen to your prescribed sound at a level where your tinnitus is still just audible.
activity.breathingWhat: Slow breathing, five minutes. Out for longer than in.
activity.symptom_checkWhat: One tap on the overview — how the day went.
activity.relaxationWhat: Progressive muscle relaxation, working from your feet upward.
activity.mindfulnessWhat: Ten minutes of attention training. The aim is not to block the sound out.
activity.sleep_routineWhat: The same fifteen minutes before bed each night — no screens, low light.
activity.sound_enrichmentWhat: Low-level background sound overnight, so the room is never silent.
activity.listening_practiceWhat: Focused listening in background noise, to retrain speech-in-noise attention.
activity.hearing_protectionWhat: Plan your day's loud exposure. Protect, but do not over-protect.

overview.title: Your dashboard
overview.body: Where you land every day. Your next appointment, a one-tap check-in, and shortcuts to everything else. It stays deliberately short — the detail lives one click away.

assessment.title: Hearing assessment
assessment.body: Start here. Three steps and about ten minutes: a few questions about you, a hearing test through your headphones, then short questionnaires. Everything else in the app is built from it.

results.title: Your results
results.body: What the assessment found, in plain language first and full clinical detail underneath. Your hearing grade, how much the tinnitus is affecting you, and what that means.

rehabilitation.title: Rehabilitation
rehabilitation.body: Your four-week recovery programme: what to do today, this week's goals, and your progress. Sound therapy is part of it, alongside breathing, relaxation and sleep work chosen from your own results.

community.title: Community
community.body: Other patients in your own city: a feed you can post to, a live chatbox, and a short reading list. Joining is your choice — until you opt in, nothing you write is visible to anyone.

group_therapy.title: Group therapy
group_therapy.body: A private room you share with a few other patients: a video call, a chatbox, and six activities you work through together — synced breathing, sound therapy and your own rehab checklist among them.

consultation.title: Consultation
consultation.body: Choose your doctor, book an appointment and join the video call. The Google Meet link appears here ten minutes before your consultation starts.

reports.title: Reports
reports.body: The full clinical report, ready to print or share with another clinician. Every number carries the method behind it and what it cannot tell you.

meet.notHeldNote: This appointment was cancelled or missed. You can book another at any time.

video.skipNote: You can watch this again any time from the Guide.

video.welcomeLead: A short video overview of the platform: what each screen is for, the order to work through them in, and how to find your way around. Everything it covers is also written out in full below.

meetNotice.title: Your consultation with {{name}} begins in {{minutes}} minutes.
meetNotice.live: Your consultation with {{name}} is starting now.

pitch.title: Which pitch is closest to your tinnitus?
pitch.instructions: A tone will play. Move the slider until it sounds as close as possible to the pitch of your own tinnitus — high or low, not loud or quiet. Use the − and + buttons for small adjustments. Nothing will match exactly; the nearest is what we want.
pitch.tip: Most people find it easier to sweep the slider from one end to the other first, get a rough idea, then fine-tune with the buttons. Your tinnitus does not stop while the tone plays — you are comparing the two.
pitch.whyBody: The frequency of your tinnitus is what your sound therapy is built around. It decides where a notch is cut and which band a masker sits in — so a good match here makes everything downstream more accurate.
pitch.levelSlider: Pitch tone level in dB HL

loudness.title: How loud is your tinnitus?
loudness.instructions: The tone is now at your matched pitch of {{hz}} Hz. Adjust the level until it is exactly as loud as your tinnitus — not louder, not quieter. Most people are surprised by how low the answer is.
loudness.tip: If the tone disappears into your tinnitus, that is the right region — nudge down until you can just tell them apart, then back up one step.
loudness.whyBody: Tinnitus is usually only a few decibels above threshold even when it feels overwhelming. That gap between the measured level and how intrusive it feels is why treatment targets the distress rather than the volume.

masking.title: Masking threshold test
masking.instructions: This is the most important measurement. For each frequency, a band of noise plays. Raise the level until your tinnitus is just covered — the moment you can no longer hear it — then press "I can no longer hear it". If it never disappears, say so; that is a real finding, not a failure.
masking.question: Can you still hear your tinnitus over this sound?
masking.notAudible: No — I can no longer hear it
masking.howBody: Start quiet and raise the level a step at a time. The point at which your tinnitus disappears is the masking threshold for that frequency. Doing this across eight frequencies shows where your tinnitus is easiest to cover — which is what your therapy sound is built from.
masking.finishPartial: Finish with what I have done

chart.title: Your masking curve
chart.label: Masking threshold against frequency
chart.legend: The shaded region is where your tinnitus is covered. The lowest point on the line is the frequency where the least sound is needed — that is your reference level.

reference.title: Reference level
reference.explain: This is the quietest sound, at the frequency where it works best, that covers your tinnitus completely. It is the level your therapy sound is set from — and it is usually much lower than people expect.
reference.selectiveNote: Your tinnitus is covered much more easily at some frequencies than others, so your therapy sound is placed precisely rather than being broadband.
reference.broadNote: Almost any sound at the right level covers your tinnitus, so your therapy can use comfortable broadband sound rather than a narrow band.
reference.insufficientNote: Test at least three frequencies to see the shape of your masking curve.
reference.not_measuredNote: The masking test was not completed.

interpretation.easily_masked: Your tinnitus is covered by a very quiet sound. That is a strong sign that sound therapy will help you.
interpretation.moderately_masked: Your tinnitus is covered at a moderate level. Sound therapy is a good fit, at a comfortable listening volume.
interpretation.hard_to_mask: Your tinnitus needs a relatively loud sound to cover it. Your programme leans on habituation and relaxation rather than raising the volume.
interpretation.above_safe: Covering your tinnitus would need a sound louder than is safe to listen to. Your programme deliberately does not try — it uses low-level enrichment and habituation instead.
interpretation.unmaskable: Your tinnitus did not disappear at any level tested. That is a meaningful finding: masking is not the right approach for you, and your programme uses habituation and relaxation instead.

combined.empty: No hearing thresholds or masking measurements to plot yet.
combined.label: Hearing thresholds with the tinnitus masking curve

monitoring.label: Daily monitoring
monitoring.title: How you have been
monitoring.todayLead: Five quick sliders. It takes about twenty seconds and it is what makes the trends below mean anything.
monitoring.alreadyLogged: You have already logged today. Adjusting the sliders and saving again replaces it.
monitoring.trendsLead: Each line compares you against your own starting point, not against anybody else. A change of less than half a point is treated as steady.
monitoring.calendarNote: Each square is a day. Filled means you did something that day — a therapy session, an activity, or a check-in.
monitoring.privacyPrivate: This is private to you. It becomes visible to a clinician only if you choose one.
monitoring.privacyShared: {{name}} can see this between your appointments, so they can review your progress without waiting for a consultation.
monitoring.lowAdherence: Adherence is below 40% for this window — worth raising at the next consultation.
monitoring.clinicianEmpty: This patient has not recorded any daily check-ins yet.

reference.title: Your personalised reference level
reference.lead: This is the last part of the hearing measurement. Rather than playing you a standard tone, we have worked out a reference tone from the measurements you have just given — your tinnitus pitch, how loud it is, and the level at which sound covers it.
reference.aboveThreshold: {{db}} dB above your own threshold here
reference.explain: Your reference tone is {{hz}} at {{db}} dB HL. Both numbers are yours: the pitch is the one you matched to your own tinnitus, and the level comes from your masking results and your hearing thresholds at that pitch. Somebody else doing this assessment would get a different tone and a different level — that is the point. A standard 1 kHz tone would sit well below where your tinnitus actually is, and everything measured against it would be less accurate for you.
reference.trimHelp: If the tone sounds noticeably too quiet or too loud, nudge it until it sits where you would expect. Most people do not need to move it at all — leaving it alone is a perfectly good answer.
reference.flooredNote: This level has been raised slightly so the tone sits above your own hearing threshold at this pitch. A reference tone you cannot hear is not a reference.
reference.cappedNote: Your measurements point to a level above {{db}} dB HL, which is louder than is safe to listen to. It has been capped, and your therapy plan will use habituation rather than trying to cover the sound.
reference.builtFromLead: Nothing here was asked twice. Every value below was taken from the assessment you have already completed.

frequencyBasis.pitch_match: The tone is set to the pitch you matched to your own tinnitus.
frequencyBasis.masking_minimum: Pitch matching was not completed, so the tone is set to the frequency where your tinnitus was covered most easily.
frequencyBasis.audiometric_notch: Pitch and masking were not completed, so the tone is set to the centre of the dip in your hearing test — which is where tinnitus most often sits.
